reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Follows a stroke, usually infarction, in the ventral posterolateral and posteromedial thalamus supplied by thalamogeniculate branches of the posterior cerebral artery
Begins with contralateral hemisensory loss that is later replaced by spontaneous, often burning, central pain on the same side
The pain is characteristically disproportionate, poorly localised, and provoked by innocuous stimuli (allodynia) or exaggerated (hyperpathia)
There is often a delay of weeks to months between the stroke and the onset of the pain syndrome
Transient contralateral hemiparesis, hemiataxia, or choreoathetosis (the so-called thalamic hand) may accompany the sensory picture
It is a prototypical central neuropathic pain disorder and responds better to neuropathic agents than to conventional analgesics
The diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging of a contralateral thalamic lesion
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome results from a lesion, typically ischaemic, of the sensory relay nuclei of the thalamus, particularly the ventral posterolateral and posteromedial nuclei supplied by thalamogeniculate perforators of the posterior cerebral artery. Loss of normal sensory processing and subsequent maladaptive reorganisation of thalamocortical and spinothalamic pathways generate spontaneous and evoked central pain. The initial hemisensory deficit reflects direct damage to the relay nuclei, while the later emergence of burning pain, allodynia, and hyperpathia reflects disinhibition and aberrant central signalling rather than ongoing peripheral input, defining it as central neuropathic pain.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral neuropathic pain or complex regional pain syndrome
Painful hemibody presentation of a brainstem or cortical stroke
Post-herpetic or other focal neuropathic pain
additionalInvestigations: MRI demonstrating a contralateral thalamic infarct or haemorrhage
Diffusion-weighted imaging in the acute phase to date the vascular event
Quantitative sensory testing to characterise the central pain profile
Vascular and stroke risk workup including ECG and metabolic profiling
MR angiography of the posterior circulation where indicated
Assessment for depression and sleep disturbance that commonly accompany chronic central pain
redFlags: New or evolving neurological deficit suggesting recurrent or extending stroke
Intractable pain driving severe depression or suicidal ideation
Features suggesting an alternative structural lesion such as tumour rather than infarct
Rapidly progressive sensory loss inconsistent with a single vascular event
reference.prognosis: The central pain is frequently chronic and difficult to control, though many patients gain partial relief with neuropathic agents and multidisciplinary pain management; spontaneous resolution is uncommon.
pitfalls: Dismissing delayed post-stroke pain as functional because it appears long after the event
Relying on simple analgesics or opioids rather than neuropathic-directed treatment
Overlooking the antecedent stroke when pain dominates the presentation
Underestimating the associated mood disturbance and its effect on pain
